turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi, Dr. [Name]. Um, well, I'm here because... lately, I've been really focused on my face. We put in this new, brighter mirror in the bathroom recently, and ever since then, I just keep noticing that the skin around my cheeks and my jawline looks... I don't know, uneven? Or kind of saggy. It's really been bothering me, even though my husband says he doesn't really see what I'm talking about when I point it out to him.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes being intensely focused on perceived uneven or saggy skin on her cheeks and jawline that bothers her, despite her husband stating he cannot see what she is referring to.

turns.doctor_question: How much has this concern about your face been affecting your daily life? For example, does it interfere with your work, relationships, or other activities?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I still get my work done, so it hasn't completely taken over. But... it is definitely having an impact. The extra time I spend getting ready in the morning, just trying to fix it or cover it up, has made me really have to rush into the courthouse a few mornings. And I've actually missed the start of my yoga class more than once lately because I just get stuck in front of the mirror.

Socially... I guess I've also been avoiding the camera. I've skipped being in a few casual photos recently, like at my book club and some community events. I just step out of the frame because I really didn't want to worry about how my face would look in them. It's just easier to avoid the pictures altogether.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient confirms ongoing preoccupation and worry about the appearance of their face, leading them to avoid being photographed.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes repetitive appearance-related behaviors, including getting stuck in front of the mirror, taking excessive time trying to fix or cover up their perceived facial flaws, and avoiding photos.

turns.doctor_question: Besides looking in the mirror, do you find yourself doing other things repeatedly to check on or try to improve how your face looks—like taking photos of yourself, comparing your face to others, or asking people for reassurance about how you look?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, I do a few of those things. Most mornings, I end up checking my face from a few different angles in the mirror. I usually put on a little extra makeup, just trying to even things out before I leave for the courthouse. 

I don't really take photos of myself, but like I mentioned, I do avoid being in casual pictures if I'm not feeling okay about how I look. And... I guess I do sometimes compare my face to the other women I see at work, just wondering if they have the same issues I'm seeing. I don't really ask for reassurance, though, besides pointing it out to my husband that one time.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient explicitly confirms engaging in repetitive appearance-related behaviors, including checking her face from multiple angles in the mirror, camouflaging with makeup, and comparing her appearance to other women.

turns.doctor_question: When you look in the mirror and see this unevenness or sagging on your cheeks and jawline, how noticeable would you say it actually is—would most people be able to see it right away, or is it something that's quite subtle or hard to notice unless you're really looking for it?
turns.patient_response:
Well, like I mentioned earlier, my husband says he can't really see what I'm talking about when I point it out to him. So... I guess to other people it must be pretty subtle, or hard to notice unless you're really looking for it. 

But for me, ever since we put that brighter mirror in the bathroom, it just stands out so much. I look at my cheeks and jaw and the sagging and unevenness are just right there. It feels obvious to me, even if no one else is really seeing it.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports being intensely focused on perceived sagging and unevenness on her cheeks and jaw that is subtle or not noticeable to others, confirming preoccupation with a perceived physical defect.

turns.doctor_question: When you're thinking about how your face looks, how much distress or anxiety does that cause you? And would you say that distress is out of proportion to how noticeable the problem actually is to other people?
turns.patient_response:
It causes me some anxiety, definitely. I mean, it bothers me enough that I'm spending extra time in the mirror and worrying about it before I leave the house. But... I wouldn't say it's completely overwhelming or ruining my life. It's just a constant, nagging frustration. 

And, yeah, considering my husband says he can't even see it, I suppose the amount of time I spend worrying about it probably is a bit out of proportion. It feels like a big deal to me, but I know logically that other people aren't staring at it the way I am.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent worry about a facial concern that her husband 'can't even see,' acknowledging her worry is out of proportion to its visibility.
symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient notes that concerns about her appearance lead her to spend extra time checking the mirror before leaving the house.
